after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
The standard matrix $T$ of a linear transformation $T$ and the vector $b\in {R}^{3}$ are given below. Determine if there exists a vector $x\in {R}^{3}$ such that $T(x)=b.$
In the affirmative case, find the value of ${x}_{1}-{x}_{2},$ where ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3}$ are the components of $x.$  

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ -2 & 3 & 1 \\ 5 & -4 & 1\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -7 \\ 7\end{aligned}]
$$
after.worked_solution:
Since $T$ is the standard matix of $T,$ we have $\text{Im}(T)=\text{Col}(T).$ In order to determine whether $b$ lies in $\text{Im}(T),$ we need to check if the equation $Tx=b$ is consistent. 

So, we find the row echelon form of the augmented matrix $[T\,|\,b],$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}[T\,|\,b] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & -1 \\ -2 & 3 & 1 & -7 \\ 5 & -4 & 1 & 7\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-5){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 3 & 3 & -9 \\ 0 & -4 & -4 & 12\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+\frac{4}{3}{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 3 & 3 & -9 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Hence ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. Now, from the second equation, we get 

$$
3{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}=-9\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=-3-{x}_{3}.
$$

From the first equation we obtain 

$$
{x}_{1}+{x}_{3}=-1\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-1-{x}_{3}.
$$

As a result, the general solution is given by 

$$
[\begin{aligned}-1-{x}_{3} \\ -3-{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{3}=2$, we have

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -5 \\ 2\end{aligned}],
$$

where $T(x)=b.$

Finally, ${x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=-3-(-5)=2.$

after.problem:
The linear transformation $T$ and the vector $b\in {R}^{4}$ are given below. Determine if there exists a vector $x\in {R}^{4}$ such that $T(x)=b.$
In the affirmative case, find the value of ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}-{x}_{4},$ where ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3},{x}_{4}$ are the components of $x.$  

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{4}\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}+2{x}_{4}+2{x}_{3} \\ 5{x}_{2}-7{x}_{4}-3{x}_{1}-{x}_{3} \\ 4{x}_{2}+{x}_{4}+5{x}_{3}+2{x}_{1} \\ -7{x}_{3}-{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}-{x}_{4}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -8 \\ -9 \\ 10\end{aligned}]
$$
after.worked_solution:
First, we write down the standard matrix of $T:$

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 & 2 \\ -3 & 5 & -1 & -7 \\ 2 & 4 & 5 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 & -7 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Since $T$ is the standard matix of $T,$ we have $\text{Im}(T)=\text{Col}(T).$ In order to determine whether $b$ lies in $\text{Im}(T),$ we need to check if the equation $Tx=b$ is consistent. 

So, let's find the row echelon form of the augmented matrix $[T\,|\,b]$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}[T\,|\,b] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 & 2 & 3 \\ -3 & 5 & -1 & -7 & -8 \\ 2 & 4 & 5 & 1 & -9 \\ -1 & -1 & -7 & -1 & 10\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{4}:={R}_{4}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 & 5 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 6 & 1 & -3 & -15 \\ 0 & -2 & -5 & 1 & 13\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-3{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{4}:={R}_{4}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 & 5 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -14 & 0 & -18 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 14\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the foruth equation, we get the false statement $0=14.$ Therefore, the system is inconsistent, and we conclude that  $b\notin \text{Im}(T).$

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
The standard matrix $T$ of a linear transformation $T$ and the vector $b\in {R}^{3}$ are given below. Determine if there exists a vector $x\in {R}^{3}$ such that $T(x)=b.$
In the affirmative case, find the value of $2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2},$ where ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3}$ are the components of $x.$  

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 5 & 7 & 9\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3 \\ 17\end{aligned}]
$$
after.worked_solution:
Since $T$ is the standard matix of $T,$ we have $\text{Im}(T)=\text{Col}(T).$ In order to determine whether $b$ lies in $\text{Im}(T),$ we need to check if the equation $Tx=b$ is consistent. 

So, we find the row echelon form of the augmented matrix $[T\,|\,b],$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}[T\,|\,b] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 & 3 \\ 5 & 7 & 9 & 17\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ 0 & -1 & -2 & -1 \\ 5 & 7 & 9 & 17\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-5){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ 0 & -1 & -2 & -1 \\ 0 & -3 & -6 & -3\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ 0 & -1 & -2 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Hence, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. 
Now, from the second equation, we get 

$$
-{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=-1\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=1-2{x}_{3}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation gives 

$$
{x}_{1}+2(1-2{x}_{3})+3{x}_{3}=4\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=2+{x}_{3}.
$$

As a result, the general solution is given by 

$$
[\begin{aligned}2+{x}_{3} \\ 1-2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{3}=0,$ we have

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],
$$

where $T(x)=b.$

Finally, $2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=2\cdot 2+1=5.$

In the affirmative case, find the value of $2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2},$ where ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3}$ are the components of $x.$  

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 5 & 7 & 9\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3 \\ 17\end{aligned}]
$$

So, we find the row echelon form of the augmented matrix $[T\,|\,b],$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}[T\,|\,b] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 & 3 \\ 5 & 7 & 9 & 17\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ 0 & -1 & -2 & -1 \\ 5 & 7 & 9 & 17\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-5){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ 0 & -1 & -2 & -1 \\ 0 & -3 & -6 & -3\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ 0 & -1 & -2 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Hence, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. 
Now, from the second equation, we get 

$$
-{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=-1\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=1-2{x}_{3}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation gives 

$$
{x}_{1}+2(1-2{x}_{3})+3{x}_{3}=4\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=2+{x}_{3}.
$$

As a result, the general solution is given by 

$$
[\begin{aligned}2+{x}_{3} \\ 1-2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],

after.problem:
Given the transformation
 $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x+y \\ 4z-2x \\ z-4x-3y\end{aligned}],$ find its rank.
after.worked_solution:
First, the standard matrix of $T$ is given by

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 4 \\ -4 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Recall that $\text{rank}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Im}(T))=\text{rank}(T).$ 

So, we need to find the rank of the matrix $T.$ We reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 4 \\ -4 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+4{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-\frac{1}{2}){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $T$ has $3$ pivot columns, we have that 

$$
\text{rank}(T)=\text{rank}(T)=3.
$$
